questions.stem:
A particle $P$ moves with constant acceleration $(2\mathbf{i}-3\mathbf{j})\,\mathrm{m\,s}^{-2}$
At time $t=0$, $P$ is moving with velocity $4\mathbf{i}\,\mathrm{m\,s}^{-1}$

parts.label: a
parts.text: (a) Find the velocity of $P$ at time $t=2$ seconds. (2)
parts.mark_scheme:
(a) Use of $\mathbf{v}=\mathbf{u}+\mathbf{a}t$ with $t=2$: $\mathbf{v}=4\mathbf{i}+2(2\mathbf{i}-3\mathbf{j})$ M1
OR integration: $\mathbf{v}=(2\mathbf{i}-3\mathbf{j})t+4\mathbf{i}$, with $t=2$ M1
$\mathbf{v}=8\mathbf{i}-6\mathbf{j}$ A1
Notes: M1: Complete method to find $\mathbf{v}$, using $\mathbf{v}=\mathbf{u}+\mathbf{a}t$ or integration (M0 if $\mathbf{i}$ and/or $\mathbf{j}$ is missing); A1: Apply isw if they also find the speed
Official notes (completeness pass):
- Accept column vectors throughout

parts.label: b
parts.text:
At time $t=0$, the position vector of $P$ relative to a fixed origin $O$ is $(\mathbf{i}+\mathbf{j})\,\mathrm{m}$.
(b) Find the position vector of $P$ relative to $O$ at time $t=3$ seconds. (2)
parts.mark_scheme:
(b) Use of $\mathbf{r}=\mathbf{u}t+\frac{1}{2}\mathbf{a}t^2$ at $t=3$: $(\mathbf{i}+\mathbf{j})+\left[3\times4\mathbf{i}+\frac{1}{2}\times(2\mathbf{i}-3\mathbf{j})\times3^2\right]$
OR: find $\mathbf{v}$ at $t=3$: $4\mathbf{i}+3(2\mathbf{i}-3\mathbf{j})=(10\mathbf{i}-9\mathbf{j})$
then use $\mathbf{r}=\frac{1}{2}(\mathbf{u}+\mathbf{v})t$
$(\mathbf{i}+\mathbf{j})+\left[\frac{1}{2}[4\mathbf{i}+(10\mathbf{i}-9\mathbf{j})]\right]\times3$
or $\mathbf{r}=\mathbf{v}t-\frac{1}{2}\mathbf{a}t^2$
$(\mathbf{i}+\mathbf{j})+\left[3\times(10\mathbf{i}-9\mathbf{j})-\frac{1}{2}\times(2\mathbf{i}-3\mathbf{j})\times3^2\right]$
OR integration: $\mathbf{r}=(\mathbf{i}+\mathbf{j})+\left[(2\mathbf{i}-3\mathbf{j})\frac{1}{2}t^2+4t\mathbf{i}\right]$, with $t=3$ M1
$\mathbf{r}=22\mathbf{i}-12.5\mathbf{j}$ A1
Notes: M1: Complete method to find the p.v. but this mark can be scored if they omit $(\mathbf{i}+\mathbf{j})$ i.e. the M1 is for the expression in the square bracket. If they integrate, the M1 is earned once the expression in the square bracket is seen with $t=3$ (M0 if $\mathbf{i}$ and/or $\mathbf{j}$ is missing); A1: cao

parts.label: a
parts.text:
2. A small stone $A$ of mass $3m$ is attached to one end of a string.
A small stone $B$ of mass $m$ is attached to the other end of the string.
Initially $A$ is held at rest on a fixed rough plane.
The plane is inclined to the horizontal at an angle $\alpha$, where $\tan\alpha=\frac{3}{4}$
The string passes over a pulley $P$ that is fixed at the top of the plane.
The part of the string from $A$ to $P$ is parallel to a line of greatest slope of the plane.
Stone $B$ hangs freely below $P$, as shown in Figure 1.
The coefficient of friction between $A$ and the plane is $\frac{1}{6}$
Stone $A$ is released from rest and begins to move down the plane.
The stones are modelled as particles.
The pulley is modelled as being small and smooth.
The string is modelled as being light and inextensible.
Using the model for the motion of the system before $B$ reaches the pulley,
(a) write down an equation of motion for $A$ (2)
parts.mark_scheme:
Mark parts (a) and (b) together.
(a) Equation of motion for $A$ M1
$3mg\sin\alpha-F-T=3ma$ A1
Notes: M1: Equation in $T$ and $a$ with correct no. of terms, condone sign errors and sin/cos confusion (If one of the 3's is missing, allow M1) N.B. Treat $\sin(3/5)$ etc as an A error but allow recovery; A1: Correct equation (allow $(-a)$ instead of $a$ in both equations)
Official notes (completeness pass):
- N.B. If m's are consistently missing treat as a MR, so max (a) M1A0 (b) M1A0B0M1A1M1A1 (c) B1B1 (d) B1
- For (a) and (b), allow verification, but must see full equations of motion.

parts.label: b
parts.text: (b) show that the acceleration of $A$ is $\frac{1}{10}g$ (7)
parts.mark_scheme:
(b) Resolve perpendicular to the plane M1
$R=3mg\cos\alpha$ A1
$F=\frac{1}{6}R$ B1
Equation of motion for $B$ OR for whole system M1
$T-mg=ma$ OR $3mg\sin\alpha-F-mg=3ma+ma$ A1
Complete method to solve for $a$ DM1
$a=\frac{1}{10}g$ * A1*
Notes: M1 (perpendicular): Correct no. of terms, condone sign errors and sin/cos confusion. Allow if appears in (a); A1: Correct equation; B1: Seen anywhere in (a) or (b), including on a diagram; M1 (equation for $B$/system): Equation (for $B$) in $T$ and $a$ with correct no. of terms, condone sign errors and sin/cos confusion OR Whole system equation with correct no. of terms, condone sign errors and sin/cos confusion; A1: Correct equation; DM1: Complete method (trig may not be substituted), dependent on M1 in (a) and second M1 in (b) if they use two equations, or second M1 in (b) if they use one equation; A1*: Correct answer correctly obtained.

parts.label: c
parts.text: (c) sketch a velocity-time graph for the motion of $B$, from the instant when $A$ is released from rest to the instant just before $B$ reaches the pulley, explaining your answer. (2)
parts.mark_scheme:
(c) [straight line starting at the origin, with positive gradient] B1
e.g. acceleration (of $B$) is constant; dependent on first B1 DB1
Notes: B1: Straight line starting at the origin (could be reflected in the $t$-axis). B0 if continuous vertical line at the end; DB1: Dependent on first B1, for any equivalent statement

parts.label: d
parts.text:
In reality, the string is not light.
(d) State how this would affect the working in part (b). (1)
parts.mark_scheme:
(d) e.g. the tensions in the two equations of motion would be different. Tension on $A$ would be different to tension on $B$ B1
Notes: B1: B0 if incorrect extras

parts.label: a
parts.text:
3. A beam $AB$ has mass $m$ and length $2a$.
The beam rests in equilibrium with $A$ on rough horizontal ground and with $B$ against a smooth vertical wall.
The beam is inclined to the horizontal at an angle $\theta$, as shown in Figure 2.
The coefficient of friction between the beam and the ground is $\mu$
The beam is modelled as a uniform rod resting in a vertical plane that is perpendicular to the wall.
Using the model,
(a) show that $\mu\geqslant\frac{1}{2}\cot\theta$ (5)
parts.mark_scheme:
Part (a) is a 'Show that...' so equations need to be given in full to earn A marks.
(a) Moments equation: (M1A0 for a moments inequality) M1
M($A$), $mga\cos\theta=2Sa\sin\theta$
M($B$), $mga\cos\theta+2Fa\sin\theta=2Ra\cos\theta$
M($C$), $F\times2a\sin\theta=mga\cos\theta$
M($D$), $2Ra\cos\theta=mga\cos\theta+2Sa\sin\theta$
M($G$), $Ra\cos\theta=Fa\sin\theta+Sa\sin\theta$ A1
($\updownarrow$) $R=mg$ OR ($\leftrightarrow$) $F=S$ B1
Use their equations (they must have enough) and $F\leqslant\mu R$ to give an inequality in $\mu$ and $\theta$ only (allow DM1 for use of $F=\mu R$ to give an equation in $\mu$ and $\theta$ only) DM1
$\mu\geqslant\frac{1}{2}\cot\theta$ * A1*
Notes: M1: Any moments equation with correct terms, condone sign errors and sin/cos confusion; A1: Correct equation; B1: Correct equation; DM1: Dependent on M1, for using their equations (they must have enough) and $F\leqslant\mu R$ to give an inequality in $\mu$ and $\theta$ only (allow M1 for use of $F=\mu R$ to give an equation in $\mu$ and $\theta$ only); A1*: Given answer correctly obtained with no wrong working seen (e.g. if they use $F=\mu R$ anywhere, A0)

parts.label: b
parts.text:
A horizontal force of magnitude $kmg$, where $k$ is a constant, is now applied to the beam at $A$.
This force acts in a direction that is perpendicular to the wall and towards the wall.
Given that $\tan\theta=\frac{5}{4}$, $\mu=\frac{1}{2}$ and the beam is now in limiting equilibrium,
(b) use the model to find the value of $k$. (5)
parts.mark_scheme:
(b) Moments equation: M1
M($A$), $mga\cos\theta=2Na\sin\theta$
M($B$), $mga\cos\theta+2kmga\sin\theta=2Ra\cos\theta+\frac{1}{2}mg\,2a\sin\theta$
M($D$), $2Ra\cos\theta=mga\cos\theta+N2a\sin\theta$
M($G$), $kmga\sin\theta+Na\sin\theta=\frac{1}{2}mga\sin\theta+Ra\cos\theta$ A1
S.C. M($C$), $mga\cos\theta+\frac{1}{2}mg\,2a\sin\theta=kmg\,2a\sin\theta$ M1A1B1
$1+\frac{5}{4}=\frac{5k}{2}$ M1
$k=0.9$ A1
$N=kmg-F$ OR $R=mg$ B1
Use their equations (they must have enough) to solve for $k$ (numerical) DM1
$k=0.9$ oe A1
Notes: M1: Any moments equation with correct terms, condone sign errors; A1: Correct equation; B1: Correct equation; DM1: Dependent on M1, for using their equations (they must have enough) with trig substituted, to solve for $k$, which must be numerical; A1: cao

parts.text:
4. A small stone is projected with speed $65\,\mathrm{m\,s}^{-1}$ from a point $O$ at the top of a vertical cliff.
Point $O$ is $70\,\mathrm{m}$ vertically above the point $N$.
Point $N$ is on horizontal ground.
The stone is projected at an angle $\alpha$ above the horizontal, where $\tan\alpha=\frac{5}{12}$
The stone hits the ground at the point $A$, as shown in Figure 3.
The stone is modelled as a particle moving freely under gravity.
The acceleration due to gravity is modelled as having magnitude $10\,\mathrm{m\,s}^{-2}$
Using the model,
(a) find the time taken for the stone to travel from $O$ to $A$, (4)
parts.mark_scheme:
Note that $g=10$; penalise once for whole question if $g=9.8$
(a) Use $s=ut+\frac{1}{2}at^2$ vertically or any complete method to give an equation in $t$ only M1
$-70=65\sin\alpha\times t-\frac{1}{2}\times g\times t^2$ A1
M(A)1
$t=7$ (s) A1
Notes: M1: Complete method, correct no. of terms, condone sign errors and sin/cos confusion; A1: Correct equation in $t$ only with at most one error; M(A)1: Correct equation in $t$ only. N.B. For 'up and down' methods etc, the two A marks are for all the equations that they use, lose a mark for each error; A1: Cao ($g=9.8$, $7.1$ or $7.11$) ($g=9.81$, $7.1$ or $7.12$)

parts.label: b
parts.text: (b) find the speed of the stone at the instant just before it hits the ground at $A$. (5)
parts.mark_scheme:
(b) Horizontal velocity component at $A=65\cos\alpha$ (60) B1
Complete method to find vertical velocity component at $A$ M1
$65\sin\alpha-g\times7$ OR $\sqrt{(-25)^2+2g\times70}$ (45) A1ft
Sub for trig and square, add and square root: $\sqrt{60^2+(-45)^2}$ M1
$75$ Accept $80\,(\mathrm{m\,s}^{-1})$ A1
Notes: B1: Seen, including on a diagram; M1: Condone sign errors and sin/cos confusion; A1ft: Correct expression; accept negative of this, follow their $t$; M1: Sub for trig and use Pythagoras; A1: Cao ($g=9.8$ or $9.81$, $75$ or $74.8$)

parts.label: c
parts.text:
One limitation of the model is that it ignores air resistance.
(c) State one other limitation of the model that could affect the reliability of your answers. (1)
parts.mark_scheme:
(c) e.g. an approximate value of $g$ has been used, the dimensions of the stone could affect its motion, spin of the stone, $g=10$ instead of $9.8$ has been used, $g$ has been assumed to be constant, wind effect, shape of the stone B1

questions.stem:
At time $t$ seconds, a particle $P$ has velocity $\mathbf{v}\,\mathrm{m\,s}^{-1}$, where
$\mathbf{v}=3t^{\frac{1}{2}}\mathbf{i}-2t\mathbf{j}\qquad t>0$

parts.label: a
parts.text: (a) Find the acceleration of $P$ at time $t$ seconds, where $t>0$ (2)
parts.mark_scheme:
Allow column vectors throughout this question.
(a) Differentiate $\mathbf{v}$ wrt $t$ M1
$\frac{3}{2}t^{-\frac{1}{2}}\mathbf{i}-2\mathbf{j}$ isw A1
Notes: M1: Both powers decreasing by 1 (M0 if vector(s) disappear but allow recovery); A1: cao

parts.label: b
parts.text: (b) Find the value of $t$ at the instant when $P$ is moving in the direction $\mathbf{i}-\mathbf{j}$ (3)
parts.mark_scheme:
(b) $3t^{\frac{1}{2}}=2t$ M1
Solve for $t$ DM1
$t=\frac{9}{4}$ A1
Notes: M1: Complete method, using $\mathbf{v}$, to obtain an equation in $t$ only, allow a sign error; DM1: Dependent on M1, solve for $t$; A1: cao

parts.label: c
parts.text:
At time $t$ seconds, where $t>0$, the position vector of $P$, relative to a fixed origin $O$, is $\mathbf{r}$ metres.
When $t=1$, $\mathbf{r}=-\mathbf{j}$
(c) Find an expression for $\mathbf{r}$ in terms of $t$. (3)
parts.mark_scheme:
(c) Integrate $\mathbf{v}$ wrt $t$ M1

questions.question_text:
At time $t$ seconds, a particle $P$ has velocity $\mathbf{v}\,\mathrm{m\,s}^{-1}$, where
$\mathbf{v}=3t^{\frac{1}{2}}\mathbf{i}-2t\mathbf{j}\qquad t>0$
(a) Find the acceleration of $P$ at time $t$ seconds, where $t>0$ (2)
(b) Find the value of $t$ at the instant when $P$ is moving in the direction $\mathbf{i}-\mathbf{j}$ (3)
At time $t$ seconds, where $t>0$, the position vector of $P$, relative to a fixed origin $O$, is $\mathbf{r}$ metres.
When $t=1$, $\mathbf{r}=-\mathbf{j}$
(c) Find an expression for $\mathbf{r}$ in terms of $t$. (3)
(d) Find the exact distance of $P$ from $O$ at the instant when $P$ is moving with speed $10\,\mathrm{m\,s}^{-1}$ (6)
